And if he seized, etc. Gidulei Terumah asks why this differs from a mortgage document that states an unspecified number of years. We rule that if the creditor remains in possession and claims three years, we do not remove the land from him because the matter is one likely to become clarified. Shach answers from Nimukei Yosef that the mortgage case is different because the borrower allowed the creditor to consume the fruits, weakening the borrower's possession. Gidulei Terumah certainly knew that Nimukei Yosef. His question is that Nimukei Yosef used that distinction only to defend Ramban's separate ruling that where a document says merely "sela'im," the debtor must still take a hesset oath if he denies owing more than two. If "sela'im" truly meant only two with certainty, why should seizure ever help in the mortgage case? But below, siman 88, we appear to accept Ramban's oath ruling. According to R. Shmuel Vidal, cited in Shitah Mekubetzet, the mortgage rule applies even where the borrower was overseas and therefore did not voluntarily allow the third year's eating. Thus the difficulty remains. The true distinction is between possession taken with permission and possession taken without permission. In the mortgage case, the creditor entered the land lawfully under the mortgage. Even if he later continues for a disputed additional period, his original possession began with permission. That is treated as possession with permission, like a tenant who lawfully occupies a bathhouse for twelve months and then claims the lease also included an intercalated month. Here, by contrast, seizure under an ambiguous loan document cannot realistically be possession with permission for the disputed amount. If the debtor gave the seized property specifically in payment of the loan, there is no dispute. If he gave it as a deposit, loaned it, or for some unrelated obligation, that is not possession with permission as to this disputed loan claim. Thus the creditor's seizure is unauthorized with respect to the disputed amount and we remove it. This resolves Gidulei Terumah's question.
We remove it from him. Shach asks from the law below, siman 54, where a receipt says merely "dinars" and can invalidate even a document for a thousand dinars. Why does broad possession help there while seizure does not help here? Bach, following Maggid Mishneh, says unspecified "dinars" can never mean more than two even in a receipt. That answer cannot fit Mechaber's law. Shach distinguishes a receipt: the witnesses intentionally wrote "dinars" generally because they did not know the amount of the underlying debt and intended the receipt to cancel whatever debt existed. That is strained. If they did not know the amount, they could simply write, "the above debt is paid." And if the receipt was written directly on the debt document, or they did know the amount, Shach's explanation fails. The better answer emerges from Tosafot at the end of Perek HaShoel. One who borrows an axe "to dig a vineyard" may use it for all his vineyards. Tosafot ask from a sale clause, "land and date palms," which is interpreted minimally. They answer, among other things, that in a sale the seller remains the possessor, whereas in a loan of movables the borrower is the possessor. Ramban accepts this possession distinction. Why then, if the creditor here has seized property, do we not say he too is the possessor? Because, as explained above, there is a difference between possession that began with permission and seizure that did not. The borrower of the axe received the object lawfully for use and seeks only to continue using it within the claimed scope of the original permission. That is possession with permission. Likewise, a mortgagor who allowed the creditor into the property gave him lawful possession. But a creditor who seizes unrelated property to satisfy an ambiguous debt did not receive possession of that property for this debt. That is unauthorized seizure and does not shift the burden. This also answers the receipt case. The debtor already possesses his own money. The creditor is trying to take it from him by saying the original debt remains unpaid. There is no stronger example of possession with permission than a person holding his own funds from before the dispute. Therefore ambiguity in the receipt can protect him far more than a creditor's later seizure can help the creditor. Still, Tosafot's first distinction, between a sale and a loan, leaves some difficulty, as do other Rishonim who distinguish land from orchards. The broader principle is the Torah rule, "If you grasped the greater amount, you have grasped nothing; grasp the lesser amount." The reason, as Tosafot explain, is that an interpretation without limit has no endpoint. In the axe case, even if we interpret "my vineyards" broadly, the maximum is finite: only the vineyards the lender owned at the time of the loan. The borrower cannot continue into future years indefinitely. Likewise in the mortgage dispute, the disputed additional consumption is bounded by what was actually eaten. But if a loan document says merely "dinars" and the creditor seeks the largest possible amount, there is no natural ceiling. A thousand, ten thousand, or all the wealth in the world could fit. Where one interpretation has no natural endpoint, the Torah rule requires adopting the minimum. This also resolves Sema's question concerning a document whose number of sela'im was accidentally erased before witnesses and the witnesses do not know what number stood there. Even though the erasure was involuntary and not the creditor's fault, seizure does not help. If we allow the creditor to claim the larger amount, there is no endpoint at all. Therefore we award only the minimum. In truth there is an additional reason. Seizure before witnesses helps principally where the document itself contains ambiguous wording. Here the document has no surviving ambiguous wording at all. The numerical content is gone. The creditor is effectively making an oral claim that the erased figure was larger. Ordinary seizure before witnesses does not validate such a bare oral uncertainty. Thus even in a witnessed accidental erasure, the creditor cannot retain more than the minimum. There is another way to see why the rule of "grasp the lesser amount" applies here. A document that says simply "dinars" contains a linguistic minimum. Hebrew plural ordinarily establishes at least two. The court therefore has a concrete floor from the document itself. If the creditor wants more, he must prove how much more. The fact that the debtor might have borrowed a much larger amount does not help because there is no textual upper endpoint. By contrast, in the axe case the language "my vineyards" identifies a closed class of objects already existing at the time of the loan. The borrower can claim the whole class because the words naturally refer to it. Likewise, in a mortgage for an unspecified period, the creditor's actual possession and consumption identify a finite disputed period. This is not an abstract possibility of limitless extension. The same distinction applies to a receipt. The receipt does not create a new affirmative claim for an unlimited amount. It is defensive. The debtor says, "Whatever claim you now bring against me has already been discharged by this writing." Since the creditor is trying to remove money from the debtor's existing possession, and the receipt directly relates to that very debt, the ambiguity operates against the creditor more readily. A loan document is the reverse. The creditor is trying to use uncertain wording to extract an affirmative additional amount. That is why identical vague plural language can have different effects in a receipt and a loan document. Accordingly, there are really three reinforcing reasons for the present ruling: the creditor's seizure is not possession with permission as to this debt; the larger interpretation has no natural endpoint; and the document itself contains no affirmative language establishing more than the minimum. Where all three are present, seizure cannot transform an uncertain claim into a right to retain the excess.

mechaber.he: כתוב בשטר פלוני לוה מפלוני כסף נותן לו חתיכ' של כסף כל דהו פחות שבמשקלות כתוב בו מטבע של כסף אם פרוטות של כסף יוצאות באותו מקום נותן לו פרוטה ואם אין פרוטות של כסף יוצאות בו נותן לו מטבע של כסף הקטן שיוצא שם ואם כתוב בו דינרי כסף או כסף דינרי נותן לו ב' דינרין של כסף ואם כתוב בו כסף בדינרי נותן לו כסף ששוה שני דינרין של זהב ואם כתוב בו זהב בדינרי נותן לו דהבא פריכא שוה שני דינרי זהב ואם כתוב בו כסף בדינרים נותן לו שברי כסף ששוה שני דינרים של כסף ואם כתוב בו זהב נותן לו חתיכה של זהב פחות שבמשקלות ואם כתוב בו מטבע של זהב נותן לו מטבע קטן היוצא של זהב כתוב בו זהב דינרים או דינרי זהב נותן לו שני דינרי זהב ואם כתוב בו זהב בדינרים נותן לו זהב שוה שני דינרין של כסף: (ועכשיו בזה"ז אין חילוק בין אמר דינרין לדינרי) (מגיד סוף ה' מלוה) (ונ"ל דנותן לו הפחות):

Dinarei. The Sema writes that the general rule in these laws is as follows. The plain term "dinarei" refers to gold dinars, while the plain term "dinarin" can refer either to silver or to gold. Since the holder of the document has the weaker hand, he receives only silver. This applies where the wording is unstated. If the document expressly says "silver dinarei" or "silver dinars," or "gold dinarin" or "gold dinars," we follow the explicit metal named. This is where no prefix meaning "in" appears. If it says "silver in dinarei," the phrase is interpreted as silver worth two gold dinars. Likewise, "gold in dinarin" means gold worth two silver dinars. According to this, the Sema emends the Mechaber's wording in the first clause and in the latter clause to preserve this grammatical distinction. The Shach writes that the text should not be emended. See there.

If it says "silver dinrei," etc. The general rule is this. The unqualified word "dinrei" ordinarily refers to gold dinars. The unqualified word "dinarin" can refer to either silver or gold, and because the holder of the document has the weaker hand, only silver is paid. But if the writing expressly says "silver dinrei," "dinrei silver," "gold dinarin," or "dinarin gold," we follow the material specified next to the noun. This applies where "dinrei" is written without the prefixed bet. If it says "silver in dinrei," the bet separates the expressions, and we interpret it as silver worth two gold dinars. Likewise "gold in dinarin" means gold worth two silver dinars. Based on this, I wrote in Perishah that in the Tur and Mechaber the first clause should read "silver dinrei" or "dinrei silver," both without a final nun, while the latter clause should read "gold dinarin" or "dinarin gold," both with a final nun. Each formulation teaches that when the material is explicitly stated, the precise form dinrei or dinarin is not decisive.

mechaber.en: If a person produces a promissory note against another for one hundred dinars or sela'im, <small>without specifying which currency,</small> then if the document was written in Babylonia he collects in Babylonian currency, and if it was written in Eretz Yisrael he collects in the currency of Eretz Yisrael. If no place is written in the document and it is produced in Babylonia, he collects in Babylonian currency; if produced in Eretz Yisrael, he collects in the local currency. If the creditor seeks to collect in the currency of the place where the document is produced and the borrower claims, "The money I owe him was of a currency worth less than this," the creditor swears and collects. <small>Rama: If the borrower brings proof that they originally lived in a place where the currency was worth less, he pays in the lesser currency.</small> If the document says merely "one hundred silver" and does not specify whether sela'im or pundeyonim, the borrower may pay whichever he chooses.

chelkat_mechokek.he: החשוד על העריות וכו'. הנה הפרש גדול יש בין בא על הערוה ממש לחשוד בעלמ' שמתייחד עם העריות דבחשוד בעלמ' נראה שאינו רק פסול מדרבנן דאינו לאו מפורש בתורה רק שהוא חשוד לאותו דבר אבל אם בא על הערוה ממש ויש עדים בדבר למאן דפסק כרב ששת (סנהדרין פז"ב דף כ"ו) הוא פסול מדאוריית' ומיהו לדעת קצת פוסקים הפוסקים כרב נחמן שם אף בבא על הערוה ממש מאחר שיצרו תוקפו כשר לעדות רק בעדות אשה נקרא חשוד מדרבנן:
chelkat_mechokek.en: One suspected of sexual immorality, etc. There is a major distinction between one who actually committed a prohibited sexual act and one merely suspected because he secludes himself with forbidden women. A person merely suspected appears to be disqualified only rabbinically, because there is no explicit Torah prohibition making him a wicked witness; he is only suspect in that area. But if he actually had relations with a forbidden woman and there are witnesses, according to those who rule like Rav Sheshet in Sanhedrin he is disqualified by Torah law. According to some authorities who rule like Rav Nachman there, even one who actually sinned may remain qualified for ordinary testimony because his inclination overcame him, although for testimony concerning a woman he is treated as suspect rabbinically.

meirat_einayim.he: ולא מתפרש איזה מטבע. נראה שמור"ם פי' דברי המחבר דר"ל אף שכתב בשטר שח"ל מאה סלעי' מ"מ לא איתפרש בהשטר באיזה מטבע ישלם לו הסלעים אם במטבע החריפים בהוצאה או לא וקאמר דבבבל מגביהו המאה סלעים ממטבע שרגילין לישא וליתן בהן בבבל כו' ופי' זה דחיתי בפרישה ע"ש וכתבתי שכוונת המחבר הוא כמ"ש המ"מ בס"פ י"ז דמלוה והוא דאף שכתב בשטר מפורש המטבע דהיינו שהלוה לו מאה דינרים או סלעים מ"מ דינר או סלע של בבל אינו דומה לסלע או דינר של א"י וה"ה לשאר ארצות דבמדינה זו היא כבידה יותר מבמדינה אחרת וכן פירש"י בהדיא במשנה בפ' בתרא דכתובות (דף ק"י ע"ב) ע"ש וע"ז קאמר שלא אתפרש דינר של איזה מקום הלוהו דמגביהו מסלע או דינר של אותו מקום שמפורש בשטר שכתבו וחתמו ואמרי' דמסתמא שם נעשה ההלואה וממטבע של אותו העיר ואם אין מפורש בשטר שום מקום מגביהו מהמטבע של מקום שמוציא בו השטר לתובעו ואמרי' מסתמא ג"כ כאן נעשה ההלואה ומדינרי של זו העיר ובסוף הסעיף כתב אם היה כתוב בו מאה כסף כו' ושם איירי במפורש בו שנעשה ההלואה במקום פלוני אלא שאין מפורש בו באיזה מטבע הלוהו וקאמר שמגביהו מה שירצה ונראה דהיינו דוקא ממטבע הקטן של אותו מקום שמפורש בשטר או של אותו מקום שמוציא בו השטר לתובעו בו ולא מטבע הקטן של שאר מקומות ועד"ר ואף דכבר כתבו המחבר בריש סי"ג ז"ל כתב בו מטבע של כסף אם פרוטות יוצאות באותו מקום כו' שם קאי אמטבע א' וכאן קמל"ן הדין במאה מטבעות:
meirat_einayim.en: And it is not explained which coinage. Rama appears to interpret the Mechaber as saying that even if the document states that he owes one hundred selaim, it does not explain which current coinage is to be used, whether the most readily accepted coins or otherwise. Thus in Bavel one would collect one hundred selaim in the currency commonly used there. I rejected this explanation in Perishah. The Mechaber's intent follows Maggid Mishneh at the end of chapter 17 of Hilchot Malveh. Even where the document expressly states the unit, such as one hundred dinars or selaim, a Babylonian dinar or sela is not equal in weight to an Eretz Yisrael dinar or sela, and similarly among other countries. Rashi explains this explicitly at the end of Ketubot. Therefore, if the document does not specify of which locality the unit was, one collects using the coin of the place identified in the document as the place where it was written and signed, because we presume the loan occurred there and used that locality's currency. If no place is stated in the document, one collects using the currency of the place where the document is produced for collection, again presuming the loan occurred there. At the end of the seif, where the document says merely "one hundred silver," the case is different. There the place of the loan is known, but the denomination itself is unspecified, so the creditor receives whichever local coin fits the wording. It appears this means the smallest coin of the place stated in the document, or if none is stated, of the place of collection, not the smallest coin from some other country. Although the Mechaber already ruled at the beginning of seif 13 that if a document says "a silver coin" and perutot circulate in that place, etc., that earlier rule concerns one coin, while this clause teaches the law of one hundred coins.

The lender swears and collects. This means that the borrower demanded, "Swear to me," which is a weaker claim than an affirmative plea of payment. Likewise, if the lender claims, "I lent you heavy currency," while the borrower seeks to repay with lighter currency according to the currency used in the place of litigation, the borrower takes a hesset oath. But if the document identifies the place where the loan was made, it is treated as certain that the loan was in the currency used there, and the borrower cannot impose an oath on the lender any more than with a claim that the document was merely a trust arrangement. If witnesses testify that the loan was made in lighter currency, the case is like two conflicting sets of witnesses.

The creditor shall swear and collect. Baal HaTerumot writes that this ruling is not clear. The Beit Yosef asks why, since the borrower's claim resembles a plea of payment, against which the creditor swears and collects. Gidulei Terumah explains that the borrower did not demand an oath, but this is unsatisfactory. The Rambam presumably also requires the oath only where the borrower says, “Swear to me,” no more than in an ordinary plea of payment. Rather, Baal HaTerumot's reason is that the creditor is believed because the ordinary presumption is that the loan was originally made as the document indicates. The borrower's contrary claim therefore resembles a claim that the note was merely one of trust, not a claim of payment. A note is ordinarily intended to stand until payment, but there is no parallel presumption supporting the borrower's allegation here. The Rambam and later authorities make this distinction in siman 82. Accordingly, the creditor should collect on the strength of his note without first taking an oath, after which the borrower may impose a hesset oath upon him. This is why Baal HaTerumot wrote that the Rambam's requirement was unclear.
However, if the borrower brought, and so forth. The Ran disagrees with this ruling. His explanation here, and his resolution of Baal HaTerumot's objection to the Rambam, are not clear to me.

אמרינן דהוי כאמנה דסתם שטר מורה על מטבע פלוני והוא אומר דאינו חייב לו רק מטבע פחות הוי כאמנה במקצת כאילו כתב בשטר שהלוהו ק' ובאמת לא הלוהו רק תשעים דמ"ש. אם כן אף עדים אלו כשכת"י אינו יוצא ממקום אחר לא יהיו נאמנים לומר דהיה מטבע פחותה דהא באמרם אמנה הוא אינם נאמנים וכן עדים אחרים יהיה כתרי נגד תרי כדלקמן בסי' מ"ו והא הסכים בעה"ת דעדים נאמנים לומר שהיו דרים מתחיל' במקום שמטבע פחותה. ועכצ"ל דאין זה בגדר אמנה דלא אסיקו עדים אדעת' אז שילך למקום אחר ממה שנעשה ההלואה ויתבע פרעון ואם כן עדיין קושי' ב"י במקומו למה לא ישבע דהא אינו דומה לאמנה ולכן נראה דבלא"ה הריטב"א והר"ן חולקים וסבירא להו דלכך לא הזכיר מקום הלואה בשטר דיהיה מחויב ליתן כל מטבע שיהיה באותו מקום שיתבענו והרב בעה"ת סבירא ליה דודאי סברתם אמת הואיל ולא הזכיר שם מקום הלואה ודאי היה תנאי ביניהם רק יד בעל השטר עה"ת אמרינן דהיה כך שיהיה יוכל לגבות בכל מקום בלי שבועה אבל לא הימנו נגד עדים וכמו נאמנות סתם דאמרינן דהימנהו לשבועה ולא נגד עדים ולכך בעדים מודה להרמב"ם ובשבועה לא בריר לי' דהא לכך לא נכתב מקום דהימנו ואם כתב מקום הלואה והוא טוען מכל מקום היה מטבע פחותה נר' דזה הוה ודאי כטוען אמנה דמ"ש אמנה במקצת או אמנה בכולו וכמש"ל ואפילו יבאו עדים ה"ל כתרי ותרי כדלקמן סי' מ"ו ואעפ"י שקצת לא משמע כן בפרישה מ"ש הדבר אמת כמ"ש. ונראה דאם הוציאו במקום שמטבע קלה שהיה שם הלוה דאין לו אלא מטבע קלה והתובע טוען מטבע כבד הלויתיך לשיטת הרמב"ם יכול להשביעו היסת אבל לפי שיטת הר"ן הוי מחילה דכך היה תנאי ולכך לשיטת הר"ן לא הוי רבי' דהא הלוהו מטבע וצ"ל דשינוי מטבע לא שכיחי ולכך לא חיישינן להו לפסול בשביל כך שטר מאוחר ודוחק. ועיין לקמן סי' ס"ט מ"ש בשטר שכתב בו סלעים דאינון וסכום המעות חלק בנייר אי נקרא שטר שיוכל לזייף ע"ש:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: The lender shall swear and collect. This is Rambam's ruling. Baal HaTerumot says the matter is not clear to him. Beit Yosef asks why this differs from an ordinary claim of repayment, where the creditor holding a document must take an oath before collecting. Shach answers that the borrower's claim resembles saying the document was a trust document. Such a claim does not ordinarily require the creditor to swear. This requires study. If the document's ordinary meaning indicates a particular currency and the borrower says he actually owes only a lower-value currency, that is like saying the document is partially a trust document: it states one hundred while only ninety were really advanced. If so, even the original document witnesses, when their signatures are not independently authenticated, should not be believed to say the currency was lower, just as witnesses are not believed to say the document was a trust document. Outside witnesses would likewise create a two-against-two situation. Yet Baal HaTerumot agrees that witnesses can establish that the parties lived in a place where the lower currency was used. Therefore this is not truly a trust-document claim. The original witnesses did not necessarily contemplate that the creditor would later sue in a different place whose currency has a different value. Their testimony was not false. Thus Beit Yosef's question remains. Ritva and Ran provide the key. They hold that the reason the document does not specify the place of the loan is that the parties implicitly agreed the debtor would pay according to the currency of whatever place the creditor later sues him. Baal HaTerumot can accept this basic reasoning yet add the principle that the holder of the document has the lower hand. The omission of the loan location shows there was an agreement concerning payment elsewhere, but the creditor was not necessarily given absolute credibility against witnesses concerning what the original currency was. Therefore, if witnesses prove the loan arose in a lower-currency place, Rambam's ruling can be accepted. But where the only challenge is the borrower's own claim, Baal HaTerumot is uncertain whether the creditor should need an oath, because the very omission may indicate that the parties trusted the document's holder regarding the place or currency. This resembles an ordinary trust clause: it can remove an oath but does not overcome witnesses. If the document expressly states the place of the loan and the borrower nevertheless says the actual currency was lower, that should be treated as a partial trust-document claim. The document explicitly says one thing and he says the substantive transaction was different. In such a case, if the original witnesses' signatures are independently authenticated, their later statement that the currency was lower should not simply overturn the document; outside witnesses would create ordinary conflicting testimony. Where the creditor sues in a place using a lighter currency and the borrower resides there, Rambam would still permit the borrower to demand a hesset oath if the creditor claims he originally lent heavier currency. According to Ran, however, the omitted location itself can be treated as a waiver or condition to pay according to the place of suit. In that model, no interest problem arises even though a lighter currency may later require repayment in heavier units elsewhere, because the agreement also carries the opposite risk. If the borrower moves to a place with even lighter currency, the lender can lose. The poskim generally follow the value of the currency at the time of the loan when the currency itself later changes in the same place. Rashba likewise writes that the operative reference point is the time of the loan, not the time of repayment. This creates a question concerning postdated documents. If the currency became heavier between the true loan date and the later date written in the document, an innocent reader could think the loan occurred under the heavier currency and require repayment accordingly, harming the borrower. Why then are postdated documents valid? Perhaps currency changes are uncommon enough that Chazal did not invalidate postdated documents for this remote concern. The answer is somewhat strained, but the law appears to require it.

Rashbam and Ri Migash, however, do not explain so; rather, a zuz is the smaller amount. Since he raised him. See Tumim, who cites Knesset HaGedolah as distinguishing that this applies only where the person who raised the child has no children of his own. Tumim writes that he does not know the source for this distinction, because the reason given in the responsa of Maimonides, that one who raises an orphan in his home is considered as though he fathered him, together with the element of affection, applies even where he has children. See there. Chatam Sofer, Even HaEzer, responsum 76, however, writes that the reasoning of Knesset HaGedolah is sound. Where a person has no children, it is natural that out of affection he might call the child “my son,” without concern that this wording could later cause damage to his heirs, since he has no children of his own and may even prefer that his beloved stepson inherit rather than his brothers or other relatives. Everyday experience supports this. But where he has biological children, he is very concerned that such wording not create a mistake that could deprive his own children of their inheritance. There is a strong presumption that a person does not abandon his own child and give to others. Therefore a document written in such terms is invalid. On this distinction Chatam Sofer also resolves Tosafot in Pesachim 54a. See there further. I cited this in Pitchei Teshuva to Even HaEzer, siman 19, seif katan 3, and see also what I wrote in Pitchei Teshuva to Yoreh Deah, siman 216, seif katan 1.

See there. See Responsa Chatam Sofer, Even HaEzer, siman 76, who writes that the reasoning of Knesset HaGedolah is sound. When a person has no sons, people sometimes call a beloved child whom they raised 'my son,' and he is not concerned that this wording will cause future harm by allowing the foster child to inherit, because he does not care so greatly whether his wife's beloved son inherits his property rather than his brothers or other relatives. Everyday experience supports this. If, however, he has sons of his own, he is very concerned that the wording not create error and loss by depriving his own sons of their inheritance. We have a presumption that a person does not abandon his own child and give his property to others. Therefore, a document written in such a form is invalid. On this basis Chatam Sofer resolves the words of Tosafos in Pesachim 54a. See there further. I cited this in Pitchei Teshuva to Even HaEzer, siman 19, seif katan 3. See also what I write in Pitchei Teshuva to Yoreh Deah, siman 216, seif katan 1.

The wording customarily used. See Responsa Maharshal, part III, simanim 46, 48, and 116, and Responsa Maharanach, end of siman 21.
Even if it was not written, it is judged as though written. The reason is that the party presumably intended the customary clause to be included. It follows plainly that this applies only when he is known to have been aware of the custom. If he did not know it, the clause is not treated as written merely because laypeople customarily include it. This explains the Rambam's ruling concerning the enactment of the Geonim that a woman may collect her ketubah from movable property. Where communities customarily write an express lien on land and movables, a ketubah written without that clause is collected from movables only if the husband knew of the enactment. When his knowledge is uncertain, the judges must deliberate carefully, because the enactment does not operate like an automatic condition of the ketubah. Where all documents omit the clause but everyone nevertheless collects from movables, a person cannot plausibly claim ignorance, since ordinary practice reveals the enactment. Where documents routinely include the clause, however, one may say that he believed collection from movables depended upon its express inclusion and deliberately omitted it. This is the Rambam's distinction and the Ribash's explanation. The Rashba indeed rules that a locally customary reservation is treated as written, like a condition imposed by beit din. Yet the Rashba also writes concerning a document designed to shield assets that even a standard formula may sometimes require proof that the woman knew the scribes used it, because one cannot assume that every woman knows technical documentary language. The matter therefore depends upon the judges' assessment. These sources show that customary wording is treated as included only when the party knew that it was ordinarily written. This is my considered view.
